entities.summary: Pope Leo VI, the 123rd bishop of Rome, was a brief but significant figure in 9th-century papal history. His pontificate, which lasted from June 928 to his death in February 929, occurred during the Saeculum obscurum, a period of relative obscurity in the history of the Catholic Church. Despite his short tenure, Leo VI played a crucial role in shaping the church's response to the Viking invasions and the Byzantine Empire's decline. He was succeeded by Pope John X, who would go on to face the challenges of a weakened papacy. Leo VI's legacy is marked by his efforts to strengthen the church's ties with the nobility and his controversial handling of the papal succession. His death in 929 marked the end of an era, as the church began to face new challenges in the 10th century. The memory of Pope Leo VI serves as a reminder of the complexities and challenges faced by the Catholic Church during its formative centuries.
